演奏時以吹管吹氣，或以風箱送氣入風袋，再以手臂壓住風袋維持穩定氣流。旋律管以兩手: You blow through a blowpipe, or a bellows feeds air into the bag, and then you press the bag with the arm to keep the airflow steady. The chanter is fingered with both hands to play the melody, and the drones are usually not fingered at all and give out a continuous chord. A beginner can practise the fingering quietly on a practice chanter, with no bag and no drones. Most chanters have an open end, so the sound does not easily stop while playing, and notes have to be separated by ornament and finger movement.

風笛以封閉簧片發聲，風袋儲存空氣並以手臂施壓調節氣流，使旋律管維持連續、均勻的聲: A bagpipe sounds with enclosed reeds; the bag stores the air and the arm presses it to regulate the flow, so the chanter keeps a continuous, even sound. Most chanters have an open end and are hard to stop while playing: phrases are usually legato, and separation and accent come mostly from finger ornament. The drones sound a continuous chord, commonly two octaves below the tonic of the chanter, with other arrangements an octave low and a fifth. Compared with a wind instrument you blow directly, a bagpipe keeps sounding while the player breathes in, because the bag supplies the air; bellows-blown pipes, whose air is not warmed and moistened by the mouth, can use finer reeds, and the reed also affects the volume.
風笛可能源自中東或中亞。約公元前400年，雅典詩人阿里斯托芬嘲諷底比斯笛手使用猛: The bagpipe may come from the Middle East or Central Asia. Around 400 BC the Athenian poet Aristophanes mocked a Theban piper for using a bag of wild-beast skin with bone pipes; the Roman emperor Nero said he played the bagpipe in public. Sources are scarce in the Dark Ages, and before the twelfth century there are only Pictish and Irish stone carvings. When it reached the British Isles is disputed; a Roman-era figurine of a piper found in England suggests the Romans may have brought it. After the Crusades of the twelfth century the bagpipe developed across Europe; from the sixteenth century the Scottish Highland bagpipe replaced the harp and travelled with the British Empire's armies to Canada, Australia and Hong Kong. The two world wars of the twentieth century made the great Highland bagpipe flourish while other traditional forms declined for a time.
風笛常見於凱爾特傳統音樂與舞蹈伴奏，也分布於歐洲、北非、西亞、波斯灣及南亞北部等: The bagpipe is common in Celtic traditional music and in dance accompaniment, and is also found in Europe, North Africa, West Asia, the Persian Gulf and the north of South Asia. The Scottish Highland bagpipe is mostly used in pipe bands and military bands, played at military funerals, major ceremonies and official parades, and it also appears in the military and police bands of former British territories such as Canada and Australia. Traditional bagpipes such as the uilleann pipes are supplied by a bag or bellows, and are used for traditional music in many places.
風笛是氣鳴樂器中的單簧管類，分類編號 422.112+422.22-62，由吹管: The bagpipe is a clarinet-type aerophone, classification number 422.112+422.22-62, made up of a blowpipe, a bag, a chanter and drones. The player blows with the mouth or works a bellows, and presses the bag with the arm to keep the sound continuous; the chanter plays the melody and the drones give out a continuous chord. It is used in the Celtic regions, Scotland, Ireland and in Europe, North Africa and West Asia, traditionally to accompany dancing, and also at military funerals, major ceremonies and performances.
風袋多以山羊、狗、羊、牛等動物皮製成，皮面常翻轉使毛朝內，並以鹽、奶、麵粉等處理: The bag is usually made of the skin of a goat, dog, sheep or cow, often turned hair-side in and treated with salt, milk or flour; synthetic materials are also found today, and the seams are sewn with a saddle stitch and a strip or else glued. The chanter is commonly boxwood, cornel, plum or another fruit wood, and also tropical hardwoods such as rosewood, ebony or African blackwood. Reeds may be cane, reed, bamboo or elder, and modern instruments also use a cotton-resin body with a clarinet reed. The source does not state the materials of the blowpipe, the stocks or the drones.
